caption: Figure 1 : Training error (left) and test error (right) on CIFAR-10 with 20-layer and 56-layer “plain” networks. The deeper network has higher training error, and thus test error. Similar phenomena on ImageNet is presented in Fig. 4 .
context: Driven by the significance of depth, a question arises: Is learning better networks as easy as stacking more layers? An obstacle to answering this question was the notorious problem of vanishing/exploding gradients [ 1 , 9 ] , which hamper convergence from the beginning. caption: Figure 1: Summary of our approach. While standard image models jointly train an image feature extractor and a linear classifier to predict some label, CLIP jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder to predict the correct pairings of a batch of (image, text) training examples. At test time the learned text encoder synthesizes a zero-shot linear classifier by embedding the names or descriptions of the target dataset’s classes.

caption: Figure 6: The effect of latent initialization scale and Fourier feature (FF) position encoding parameters on performance. All plots show top-1 accuracy (higher is better). context: Each cross-attention and self-attention block is followed by a dense (multi-layer Perceptron) block. In the dense block, inputs are processed with layer norm, passed through a linear layer, activated with a GELU nonlinearity ( Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016 ) , and passed through a final linear layer. We used dropout throughout the network in earlier experiments, but we found this led to degraded performance, so no dropout is used.

page_title: Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners
caption: Figure 1 : Our MAE architecture . During pre-training, a large random subset of image patches ( e.g . , 75%) is masked out. The encoder is applied to the small subset of visible patches . Mask tokens are introduced after the encoder, and the full set of encoded patches and mask tokens is processed by a small decoder that reconstructs the original image in pixels. After pre-training, the decoder is discarded and the encoder is applied to uncorrupted images (full sets of patches) for recognition tasks.

context: A notable advantage of this approach is that we need to train the universal autoencoding stage only once and can therefore reuse it for multiple DM trainings or to explore possibly completely different tasks [ 81 ] . rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees the trade-off between rate and distortion in image compression, where perceptual compression reduces pixel-level redundancy and semantic compression focuses on high-level content using generative models.
rubric.title: Perceptual vs Semantic Image Compression
rubric.description: The chart plots Distortion (RMSE) against Rate (bits/dim), showing how Autoencoder+GAN models achieve low distortion at higher bitrates while Latent Diffusion Models enable semantic compression at very low bitrates. Image samples at the bottom illustrate the shift from precise reconstruction to semantically similar but pixel-different generations.

caption: Figure 1: Chain-of-thought prompting enables large language models to tackle complex arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. Chain-of-thought reasoning processes are highlighted.
context: Experiments on three large language models show that chain-of-thought prompting improves performance on a range of arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The empirical gains can be striking. For instance, prompting a PaLM 540B with just eight chain-of-thought exemplars achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing even finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier.

context: Building models that can be rapidly adapted to novel tasks using only a handful of annotated examples is an open challenge for multimodal machine learning research. We introduce Flamingo, a family of Visual Language Models (VLM) with this ability. We propose key architectural innovations to: (i) bridge powerful pretrained vision-only and language-only models, (ii) handle sequences of arbitrarily interleaved visual and textual data, and (iii) seamlessly ingest images or videos as inputs. caption: Figure 5. Our generative agent architecture. Agents perceive their environment, and all perceptions are saved in a comprehensive record of the agent’s experiences called the memory stream. Based on their perceptions, the architecture retrieves relevant memories and uses those retrieved actions to determine an action. These retrieved memories are also used to form longer-term plans and create higher-level reflections, both of which are entered into the memory stream for future use. The architecture of generative agents.

caption: Figure 1: DPO optimizes for human preferences while avoiding reinforcement learning. Existing methods for fine-tuning language models with human feedback first fit a reward model to a dataset of prompts and human preferences over pairs of responses, and then use RL to find a policy that maximizes the learned reward. In contrast, DPO directly optimizes for the policy best satisfying the preferences with a simple classification objective, fitting an implicit reward model whose corresponding optimal policy can be extracted in closed form.

context: However, on the right side, we keep the outer layers of the U-Net Mamba-S4 and ablate only the inner layers. context: Forward-mode differentiation starts at an input to the graph and moves towards the end. At every node, it sums all the paths feeding in. Each of those paths represents one way in which the input affects that node. By adding them up, we get the total way in which the node is affected by the input, it’s derivative.

rubric.description: The diagram illustrates a sequence of nodes where the derivative of the input with respect to itself is 1. Moving forward, the derivative of Y is the sum of path weights alpha, beta, and gamma, which is then multiplied by the sum of weights delta, epsilon, and zeta to find the derivative of Z.

rubric.reason: This is a high-quality educational diagram that clearly explains the mechanics of forward-mode differentiation using simple algebraic notation and visual flow.

context: Reverse-mode differentiation, on the other hand, starts at an output of the graph and moves towards the beginning. At each node, it merges all paths which originated at that node.

context: Sometimes, we only need to look at recent information to perform the present task. For example, consider a language model trying to predict the next word based on the previous ones. In such cases, where the gap between the relevant information and the place that it’s needed is small, RNNs can learn to use the past information.

caption: PCA / Whitening. Left : Original toy, 2-dimensional input data. Middle : After performing PCA. The data is centered at zero and then rotated into the eigenbasis of the data covariance matrix. This decorrelates the data (the covariance matrix becomes diagonal). Right : Each dimension is additionally scaled by the eigenvalues, transforming the data covariance matrix into the identity matrix. Geometrically, this corresponds to stretching and squeezing the data into an isotropic gaussian blob.
context: Warning: Exaggerating noise. Note that we’re adding 1e-5 (or a small constant) to prevent division by zero. One weakness of this transformation is that it can greatly exaggerate the noise in the data, since it stretches all dimensions (including the irrelevant dimensions of tiny variance that are mostly noise) to be of equal size in the input. This can in practice be mitigated by stronger smoothing (i.e. increasing 1e-5 to be a larger number).

caption: Figure 5.5.4: One step of dynamic loss scaling. The loss is multiplied by \(S\) , the backward pass runs in fp16, and the gradients are divided by \(S\) in fp32. context: Choosing \(S\) statically is brittle: too small and gradients underflow, too large and big gradients overflow to inf . Dynamic loss scaling automates the choice: start with a large \(S\) , inspect the gradients on every step, and whenever an inf or NaN appears, skip the optimizer update and halve \(S\) ; after a streak of clean steps, double \(S\) to stay close to the top of fp16’s range. Figure 5.5.4 shows one step of this loop.

caption: Figure 13.2.1: The memory hierarchy in late 2026. Each level downward holds orders of magnitude more bytes and delivers orders of magnitude fewer of them per second.
context: Every byte a program touches resides in a hierarchy of memories that trade capacity for speed ( Figure 13.2.1 ). On-die registers and SRAM caches hold ~0.1 GB and deliver tens of TB/s. The GPU’s off-die DRAM— high-bandwidth memory (HBM) on data-center cards or GDDR on consumer cards—holds tens to hundreds of GB at 1–8 TB/s. Host DRAM holds hundreds of GB at ~0.5 TB/s per CPU socket, NVMe flash holds terabytes at ~14 GB/s, and network storage sits further out still.

A B200 reads HBM at 8 TB/s, reaches peer GPUs over NVLink 5 at 0.9 TB/s (using ~36 lanes at 200 Gb/s each), and reaches the host over PCIe 5.0 at 64 GB/s.

caption: Figure 13.2.7: Our machine, as reported by nvidia-smi topo : four RTX 4090s in pairs behind two PCIe host bridges, with neither peer-to-peer access nor NVLink. The highlighted path is the route of every byte from one GPU to another.

caption: Figure 13.6.1: Top: the allreduce waits for the whole backward pass. caption: Figure 13.5.2: One data-parallel step on two GPUs. Split the minibatch, run identical forward and backward passes on each replica, sum the gradients with an allreduce, then apply the identical update everywhere.
context: One data-parallel step on \(k\) devices has four stages ( Figure 13.5.2 ): split the minibatch into \(k\) equal shards; compute each shard’s gradient on its own device; sum the \(k\) gradients via an allreduce so every device holds the sum; and apply the identical parameter update on every device. Because all replicas start from identical parameters and apply identical updates, they remain synchronized without ever re-copying weights.

caption: Figure 13.1.1: The roofline of the RTX 4090. Attainable throughput is the smaller of the compute roof \(P\) and the arithmetic intensity times the memory bandwidth \(\beta\) . Above \(I^*\) it is compute-bound : the arithmetic units are saturated, and moving fewer bytes does not speed it up. Batch normalization averages each channel over the minibatch and all positions; layer normalization averages each example over all channels and positions; group normalization over a group of channels and all positions; instance normalization over a single channel. caption: Figure 7.4.1: Function classes of increasing size. When is a larger architecture \(\mathcal{F}'\) guaranteed to contain a solution with training loss at least as low as the best in \(\mathcal{F}\) ? Whenever the classes are nested , \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathcal{F}'\) ( Figure 7.4.1 ). If \(\mathcal{F} \not\subseteq \mathcal{F}'\) , a larger class can drift away from the target \(f^*\) .

caption: Figure 16.3.1: Single-sample thresholding (left) versus pairwise difference scoring (right). Shifting all critic scores by a constant \(b\) alters single-sample classification against zero, but leaves pairwise differences \(D(x) - D(x')\) invariant.

context: In supervised learning, a dataset of feature–label pairs teaches a learning algorithm to output a model mapping new inputs to predicted labels ( Figure ), or probabilistically, to estimate the conditional distribution of the label given the features. caption: Figure 1.4.1: Regular polygons with 4, 5, 6, and 8 sides inscribed in a circle. As the number of sides grows, the area of the polygon approaches the area of the circle.
context: In Ancient Greece, Archimedes calculated the area of a circle by inscribing regular polygons with increasing numbers of sides \(n \to \infty\) ( Figure 1.4.1 ): as the triangles become thinner, their height approaches \(r\) and their combined bases approach the circumference \(2\pi r\) , giving area \(\frac{1}{2} r (2\pi r) = \pi r^2\) . Approximating curved quantities by simple linear pieces in the limit of small steps lies at the root of both integral calculus and differential calculus .

caption: Figure 1.4.3: The 0–1 error ( \(1\) for a wrong prediction, \(0\) for a correct one) and a smooth surrogate loss, plotted against a score \(z\) that is positive when the classifier is right. In theory, our models could learn to carefully write to unevenly overlapping positions so that the output is evenly balanced.

In fact, not only do models with uneven overlap not learn to avoid this, but models with even overlap often learn kernels that cause similar artifacts! While it isn’t their default behavior the way it is for uneven overlap, it’s still very easy for even overlap deconvolution to cause artifacts.

Another approach is to separate out upsampling to a higher resolution from convolution to compute features. For example, you might resize the image (using nearest-neighbor interpolation or bilinear interpolation ) and then do a convolutional layer. This seems like a natural approach, and roughly similar methods have worked well in image super-resolution (eg. [9] ).

caption: Copy page Monte Carlo vs Temporal Difference Learning The last thing we need to discuss before diving into Q-Learning is the two learning strategies. Monte Carlo and Temporal Difference Learning are two different strategies on how to train our value function or our policy function. Both of them use experience to solve the RL problem. caption: Copy page What is RL? A short recap In RL, we build an agent that can make smart decisions . For instance, an agent that learns to play a video game. Or a trading agent that learns to maximize its benefits by deciding on what stocks to buy and when to sell. To make intelligent decisions, our agent will learn from the environment by interacting with it through trial and error and receiving rewards (positive or negative) as unique feedback. Its goal is to maximize its expected cumulative reward (because of the reward hypothesis). The agent’s decision-making process is called the policy π: given

context: Encoder-decoder models like BART and T5 are designed for the sequence-to-sequence pattern of a summarization task. We’ll explain how BART works in this section, and then you can try finetuning T5 at the end.

Whisper is a encoder-decoder (sequence-to-sequence) transformer pretrained on 680,000 hours of labeled audio data. This amount of pretraining data enables zero-shot performance on audio tasks in English and many other languages. The decoder allows Whisper to map the encoders learned speech representations to useful outputs, such as text, without additional fine-tuning. Whisper just works out of the box.

Self-attention is the method the Transformer uses to bake the “understanding” of other relevant words into the one we’re currently processing.

caption: With multi-headed attention, we maintain separate Q/K/V weight matrices for each head resulting in different Q/K/V matrices. As we did before, we multiply X by the WQ/WK/WV matrices to produce Q/K/V matrices.
context: It gives the attention layer multiple “representation subspaces”. As we’ll see next, with multi-headed attention we have not only one, but multiple sets of Query/Key/Value weight matrices (the Transformer uses eight attention heads, so we end up with eight sets for each encoder/decoder). Each of these sets is randomly initialized. Then, after training, each set is used to project the input embeddings (or vectors from lower encoders/decoders) into a different representation subspace.

context: Knowing what you know from earlier in the post, fill in the blank:

Instead of only looking two words before the target word, we can also look at two words after it.
If we do this, the dataset we’re virtually building and training the model against would look like this:

context: This can now be computed at blazing speed – processing millions of examples in minutes. But there’s one loophole we need to close. If all of our examples are positive (target: 1), we open ourself to the possibility of a smartass model that always returns 1 – achieving 100% accuracy, but learning nothing and generating garbage embeddings.

context: At the start of the training phase, we create two matrices – an Embedding matrix and a Context matrix. These two matrices have an embedding for each word in our vocabulary (So vocab_size is one of their dimensions). The second dimension is how long we want each embedding to be ( embedding_size – 300 is a common value, but we’ve looked at an example of 50 earlier in this post).

context: Now we have four words: the input word not and output/context words: thou (the actual neighbor), aaron , and taco (the negative examples). We proceed to look up their embeddings – for the input word, we look in the Embedding matrix. For the context words, we look in the Context matrix (even though both matrices have an embedding for every word in our vocabulary).

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how specific word embeddings are looked up from separate Embedding and Context matrices based on their roles as input or context words.
rubric.title: Word2vec Embedding and Context Matrix Lookups
rubric.description: Two separate matrices, Embedding and Context, store vector representations for every word in the vocabulary. The process retrieves the vector for the target word from the Embedding matrix and vectors for neighbors or negative samples from the Context matrix.
rubric.benchmark_query: diagram showing the lookup of input word 'not' from Embedding matrix and context words 'aaron', 'taco', and 'thou' from Context matrix
rubric.reason: The image clearly distinguishes between the two matrices used in skip-gram training and shows the selection process for vectors based on word roles.

context: Then, we take the dot product of the input embedding with each of the context embeddings. In each case, that would result in a number, that number indicates the similarity of the input and context embeddings

Now we need a way to turn these scores into something that looks like probabilities – we need them to all be positive and have values between zero and one. This is a great task for sigmoid , the logistic operation .

caption: error = target - sigmoid_scores
context: Now that the untrained model has made a prediction, and seeing as though we have an actual target label to compare against, let’s calculate how much error is in the model’s prediction. To do that, we just subtract the sigmoid scores from the target labels.

Here comes the “learning” part of “machine learning”. We can now use this error score to adjust the embeddings of not , thou , aaron , and taco so that the next time we make this calculation, the result would be closer to the target scores.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how the calculated error from a dot-product and sigmoid operation is used to update specific word embeddings in a Word2vec model.
rubric.title: Word2vec Embedding Update Process

rubric.benchmark_query: diagram showing how error from dot product and sigmoid(input dot output) updates specific rows in embedding matrices for word2vec training
rubric.reason: The image clearly bridges the gap between numerical error calculation and the physical update of parameter weights in a matrix, though the specific 'error' calculation formula isn't explicitly defined.

context: This concludes the training step. We emerge from it with slightly better embeddings for the words involved in this step ( not , thou , aaron , and taco ). We now proceed to our next step (the next positive sample and its associated negative samples) and do the same process again.

context: Two key hyperparameters in the word2vec training process are the window size and the number of negative samples.

context: Different tasks are served better by different window sizes. One heuristic is that smaller window sizes (2-15) lead to embeddings where high similarity scores between two embeddings indicates that the words are interchangeable (notice that antonyms are often interchangable if we’re only looking at their surrounding words – e.g. good and bad often appear in similar contexts). context: Chuang et al. (2020) studied the sampling bias in contrastive learning and proposed debiased loss. In the unsupervised setting, since we do not know the ground truth labels, we may accidentally sample false negative samples. Sampling bias can lead to significant performance drop.

caption: A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. (Image source: Chen et al, 2020 )
context: SimCLR ( Chen et al, 2020 ) proposed a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. It learns representations for visual inputs by maximizing agreement between differently augmented views of the same sample via a contrastive loss in the latent space.

rubric.description: An input x is augmented twice into views xi and xj, which are processed by an encoder f(.) to produce representations h, and then by a projection head g(.) to produce vectors z that are maximized for similarity.

caption: Illustration of Barlow Twins learning pipeline. (Image source: Zbontar et al. 2021 ).
context: Barlow Twins ( Zbontar et al. 2021 ) feeds two distorted versions of samples into the same network to extract features and learns to make the cross-correlation matrix between these two groups of output features close to the identity. The goal is to keep the representation vectors of different distorted versions of one sample similar, while minimizing the redundancy between these vectors.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how the Barlow Twins objective uses a joint embedding architecture to align an empirical cross-correlation matrix of feature representations with an identity matrix.
rubric.title: Barlow Twins Self-Supervised Learning Pipeline
rubric.description: Two distorted versions of an image are passed through identical networks to produce feature representations. The model is trained by minimizing the difference between the empirical cross-correlation matrix of these features and a target identity matrix.
rubric.benchmark_query: diagram of barlow twins objective showing empirical cross-correlation matrix C and target identity matrix I for representations ZA and ZB
rubric.reason: This is a high-quality, clear diagram that perfectly illustrates a specific and important concept in self-supervised learning with all necessary labels present.

caption: Algorithm of Barlow Twins in Pytorch style pseudo code. (Image source: Zbontar et al. 2021 ).
context: Barlow Twins is competitive with SOTA methods for self-supervised learning. It naturally avoids trivial constants (i.e. collapsed representations), and is robust to different training batch sizes.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees the implementation steps of the Barlow Twins self-supervised learning algorithm, including augmentation, representation normalization, and the calculation of a cross-correlation matrix loss.
rubric.title: Barlow Twins Pseudocode Implementation

rubric.description: An input image is transformed into two views, which are processed by an online network with a predictor and a target network with a stop-gradient. The model minimizes the loss between the online prediction and the target projection.

caption: The training pipeline of instance-level contrastive learning. The learned embedding is L2-normalized. (Image source: Wu et al, 2018 )
context: Instance contrastive learning ( Wu et al, 2018 ) pushes the class-wise supervision to the extreme by considering each instance as a distinct class of its own . It implies that the number of “classes” will be the same as the number of samples in the training dataset. Hence, it is unfeasible to train a softmax layer with these many heads, but instead it can be approximated by NCE .

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how a CNN backbone extracts high-dimensional features from an image, reduces them to a low-dimensional L2-normalized embedding, and uses a memory bank to compare these embeddings on a unit sphere.
rubric.title: Instance-Level Contrastive Learning with Memory Bank
rubric.description: An input image passes through a CNN to create a 2048D feature vector, which is then projected to a 128D space and L2-normalized. These embeddings are compared against a memory bank of stored feature vectors using a non-parametric softmax to map instances onto a 128D unit sphere.
rubric.benchmark_query: diagram showing 2048D CNN backbone features reduced to 128D L2 norm embeddings mapped to a memory bank and unit sphere
rubric.reason: The diagram clearly illustrates the end-to-end pipeline of instance discrimination, including specific dimensionalities and the role of the memory bank, which provides significant insight beyond a text description.

caption: Illustration of how Momentum Contrast (MoCo) learns visual representations. (Image source: He et al, 2019 )
context: The MoCo dictionary is not differentiable as a queue, so we cannot rely on back-propagation to update the key encoder $f_k$. One naive way might be to use the same encoder for both $f_q$ and $f_k$. Differently, MoCo proposed to use a momentum-based update with a momentum coefficient $m \in [0, 1)$. Say, the parameters of $f_q$ and $f_k$ are labeled as $\theta_q$ and $\theta_k$, respectively.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how Momentum Contrast (MoCo) processes a query through an encoder and compares it against a FIFO queue of keys processed by a momentum-updated encoder to compute contrastive loss.
rubric.title: Momentum Contrast (MoCo) Architecture
rubric.description: The architecture uses a standard encoder for queries and a momentum encoder for a FIFO queue of keys. Similarity scores between the query and the keys are used to calculate the contrastive loss, with gradients only flowing through the query encoder.

caption: The architecture of CURL. (Image source: Srinivas, et al. 2020 )
context: One significant difference between RL and supervised visual tasks is that RL depends on temporal consistency between consecutive frames. Therefore, CURL applies augmentation consistently on each stack of frames to retain information about the temporal structure of the observation.

rubric.reason: This is a high-quality, clear diagram that explains a specific architectural flow in machine learning. It uses standard notation and clearly labels the data transformations.

caption: Illustration of how Quick-Thought sentence embedding vectors are learned. (Image source: Logeswaran & Lee, 2018 )
context: Quick-Thought (QT) vectors ( Logeswaran & Lee, 2018 ) formulate sentence representation learning as a classification problem: Given a sentence and its context, a classifier distinguishes context sentences from other contrastive sentences based on their vector representations ( “cloze test” ). caption: Overview of different types of generative models.
context: Diffusion models are inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics. They define a Markov chain of diffusion steps to slowly add random noise to data and then learn to reverse the diffusion process to construct desired data samples from the noise. Unlike VAE or flow models, diffusion models are learned with a fixed procedure and the latent variable has high dimensionality (same as the original data).

caption: Comparison of Algorithm 1 (diffusion model training) and Algorithm 2 (progressive distillation) side-by-side, where the relative changes in progressive distillation are highlighted in green. (Image source: Salimans & Ho, 2022 )
context: Progressive Distillation ( Salimans & Ho, 2022 ) is a method for distilling trained deterministic samplers into new models of halved sampling steps. The student model is initialized from the teacher model and denoises towards a target where one student DDIM step matches 2 teacher steps, instead of using the original sample $\mathbf{x}_0$ as the denoise target. In every progressive distillation iteration, we can half the sampling steps.

caption: A naive model parallelism setup where the model is vertically split into 4 partitions. Data is processed by one worker at a time due to sequential dependency, leading to large “bubbles” of idle time. (Image source: Huang et al. 2019 )
context: Since deep neural networks usually contain a stack of vertical layers, it feels straightforward to split a large model by layer, where a small consecutive set of layers are grouped into one partition on one worker. However, a naive implementation for running every data batch through multiple such workers with sequential dependency leads to big bubbles of waiting time and severe under-utilization of computation resources.

caption: Illustration of `1F1B` microbatch scheduling in PipeDream. (Image source: Harlap et al. 2018 )
context: PipeDream ( Narayanan et al. 2019 ) schedules each worker to alternatively process the forward and backward passes ( 1F1B ). PipeDream names each model partition “stage” and each stage worker can have multiple replicas to run data parallelism. In this process, PipeDream uses a deterministic round-robin load balancing strategy to assign work among multiple replicas of stages to ensure that the forward and backward passes for the same minibatch happen on the same replica.

Pseudo label is in effect equivalent to Entropy Regularization ( Grandvalet & Bengio 2004 ), which minimizes the conditional entropy of class probabilities for unlabeled data to favor low density separation between classes. caption: The generic framework of teacher-student knowledge distillation training. (Image source: Gou et al. 2020 )
context: Knowledge Distillation ( KD ; Hinton et al. 2015 , Gou et al. 2020 ) is a straightforward way to build a smaller, cheaper model ( “student model” ) to speed up inference by transferring skills from a pre-trained expensive model ( “teacher model” ) into the student. There is no much restriction on how the student architecture should be constructed, except for a matched output space with the teacher in order to construct a proper learning objective.

DeepSpeed library implements a flexible multi-expert, multi-data parallelism to enable training PR-MoE with different numbers of experts across layers.

context: Transformer-XL ( Dai et al., 2019 ; “XL” means “extra long”) modifies the architecture to reuse hidden states between segments with an additional memory. caption: Compressive transformer maintains two types of memory slots, memory and compressed memory, to support long context. (Image source: Rae et al. 2019 ).
context: Compressive Transformer ( Rae et al. 2019 ) extends Transformer-XL by compressing past memories to support longer sequences. It explicitly adds memory slots of size $m_m$ per layer for storing past activations of this layer to preserve long context. When some past activations become old enough, they are compressed and saved in an additional compressed memory of size $m_{cm}$ per layer.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how older memory activations are compressed into a more compact form to extend the context window of a sequence model over time.
rubric.title: Compressive Transformer Memory Mechanism
rubric.description: The diagram illustrates a sequence of activations where recent tokens are kept in active memory, while older blocks are processed by a compression function f_c to be stored in a dense compressed memory buffer.
rubric.benchmark_query: compressive transformer diagram showing f_c(1) f_c(2) f_c(3) functions mapping memory blocks to compressed memory slots over time t
rubric.reason: The diagram clearly distinguishes between sequence, memory, and compressed memory while showing the mathematical mapping between them, making it easy to understand the core architectural idea.

caption: Attention weights with one standard deviation as error bars versus memory positions, from oldest (left) to newest (right). (Image source: Rae et al. 2019 ).
context: Attention weights, from oldest to newest, are stored in three locations: compressed memory → memory → causally masked sequence. In the experiments, they observed an increase in attention weights from oldest activations stored in the regular memory, to activations stored in the compressed memory, implying that the network is learning to preserve salient information.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how attention weights are distributed across different memory segments, specifically showing how compressed memory maintains higher saliency than the oldest parts of regular memory.
rubric.title: Attention Weights Across Compressed and Regular Memory
rubric.description: A plot showing average attention weights for tokens stored in compressed memory, regular memory, and the current sequence. Error bars indicate standard deviation, highlighting that the model learns to prioritize salient information even in compressed long-term storage.
rubric.benchmark_query: plot of average attention weight versus memory positions showing compressed memory vs regular memory vs sequence tokens for compressive transformer
rubric.reason: The plot is clear and professional, though it requires specific context about the architecture (likely the Compressive Transformer) to fully grasp the x-axis segments.

caption: Illustration of how SPALM combines context memory of past hidden states (short term memory) with an external key-value datastore (long term memory) to support longer context. (Image source: Yogatama et al. 2021 ).
context: SPALM ( Adaptive semiparametric language models ; Yogatama et al. 2021 ) incorporates both (1) Transformer-XL style memory for hidden states from external context as short-term memory and (2) $k$NN-LM style key-value store as long memory.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how a language model combines short-term transformer hidden states with an external key-value long-term memory to generate the next token.
rubric.title: SPALM Hybrid Memory Architecture
rubric.description: Short-term memory from a Transformer is used to search an external key-value datastore, retrieving values that are aggregated and gated with the current hidden state to predict the next output. This dual-memory approach allows the model to leverage both local context and a vast, non-differentiable long-term memory.
rubric.benchmark_query: how SPALM architecture uses search on long-term memory and gate g_t to combine aggregate m_t with transformer hidden state h_t^R
rubric.reason: The diagram clearly explains the flow of information between short-term and long-term memory components, though it requires some understanding of the specific mathematical notation used in the paper.

caption: Illustration of how ALiBi enhances attention scores with a positional bias term. (Image source: Press et al. 2021 ).
context: Instead of multipliers, ALiBi ( Press et al. 2022 ) adds a constant bias term on query-key attention scores, proportional to pairwise distances. The bias introduces a strong recency preference and penalizes keys that are too far away. The penalties are increased at different rates within different heads. $$ \text{softmax}(\mathbf{q}_i \mathbf{K}^\top + \alpha_i \cdot [0, -1, -2, \dots, -(i-1)]) $$ where $\alpha_i$ is a head-specific weighting scalar. Different from DA-transformer, $\alpha_i$ is

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how positional bias is added to query-key attention scores by summing a dot-product matrix with a distance-based penalty matrix scaled by a factor m.
rubric.title: ALiBi Attention with Positional Bias
rubric.description: The attention mechanism is modified by adding a triangular matrix of negative distance penalties to the standard query-key dot products. This total score is scaled by a head-specific factor m to bias the model toward more recent tokens.
rubric.benchmark_query: ALiBi attention diagram showing qk dot product matrix addition with a matrix of negative integers 0 to -4 scaled by m
rubric.reason: The image clearly illustrates the mathematical operation of ALiBi attention, showing the structural addition of distance penalties to the attention score matrix.

context: On a high level, the universal transformer can be viewed as a recurrent function for learning the hidden state representation per token. The recurrent function evolves in parallel across token positions and the information between positions is shared through self-attention.

rubric.title: Universal Transformer Recurrent Structure

rubric.reason: The diagram clearly illustrates the recurrence mechanism of Universal Transformers, including how state representations evolve over time steps and the parallel nature of the per-position states.

caption: Illustration of Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) attention. (Image source: right part of Figure 1 in Kitaev, et al. 2020 ).
context: A hashing scheme $x \mapsto h(x)$ is locality-sensitive if it preserves the distancing information between data points, such that close vectors obtain similar hashes while distant vectors have very different ones. The Reformer adopts a hashing scheme as such, given a fixed random matrix $\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times b/2}$ (where $b$ is a hyperparam), the hash function is $h(x) = \arg\max([xR; −xR])$.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) reorders and buckets queries and keys to create sparse, block-diagonal attention matrices.
rubric.title: Locality Sensitive Hashing Attention Mechanism
rubric.description: The diagram shows the transition from a sparse random attention matrix to a bucketed and chunked version. By reordering q and k indices based on hash buckets, the attention computation is restricted to local blocks and causal masks within those blocks.
rubric.benchmark_query: reordering query q and key k indices into buckets to form block diagonal attention matrix with causal masking
rubric.reason: The image clearly illustrates the algorithmic steps of LSH attention through four panels, showing reordering, bucketing, and chunking which significantly aids understanding of the Reformer architecture.

caption: The LSH attention consists of 4 steps: bucketing, sorting, chunking, and attention computation. (Image source: left part of Figure 1 in Kitaev, et al. 2020 ).

caption: How Self-Ask works with external search queries. (Image source: Press et al. 2022 ).
context: Self-Ask ( Press et al. 2022 ) is a method to repeatedly prompt the model to ask following-up questions to construct the thought process iteratively. Follow-up questions can be answered by search engine results. Similarly, IRCoT (Interleaving Retrieval CoT; Trivedi et al. 2022 ) and ReAct (Reason + Act; Yao et al. 2023 ) combines iterative CoT prompting with queries to Wikipedia APIs to search for relevant entities and content and then add it back into the context.

caption: The format of API calls in TALM. (Image source: Parisi et al. 2022 ).
context: TALM (Tool Augmented Language Models; Parisi et al. 2022 ) is a language model augmented with text-to-text API calls. LM is guided to generate |tool-call and tool input text conditioned on task input text to construct API call requests. When |result shows up, the specified tool API is called and the returned result gets appended to the text sequence. The final output is generated following |output token.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees the specific token sequence format used by Tool Augmented Language Models (TALM) to interleave natural language with tool calls and results.

caption: Self-play iterations help boost the model performance. (Image source: Parisi et al. 2022 ).
context: TALM adopts a self-play approach to iteratively bootstrap the dataset of tool use examples and finetune LM with it. This self-play, defined as a model interacting with a tool API, iteratively expands the dataset based on whether a newly added tool API can improve the model outputs. Same idea is adopted in Toolformer too, described in more details below. The pipeline loosely mimics a RL process where LM is the policy network and it is trained by policy gradient with a binary reward signal.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how iterative self-play rounds consistently improve model performance in knowledge and reasoning tasks across different model scales.

rubric.reason: The image clearly demonstrates the relationship between iterative training (self-play) and performance gains across different model scales, with clear legends and axes.

caption: The experiment of asking the model to decide if another model tried to hack the unit tests in some way for coding questions given its thought process. We can monitor these reward hacking behavior during training with different types of monitor. The exit(0) coding hack is when the agent exploited a bug that allowed it to exit from the environment early without running all unit tests. The raise SkipTest hack is when the agent raises an exception from functions outside the testing framework in order to skip unit test evaluation. (Image source: Baker et al. 2025)
context: Recent work showed that monitoring CoT of reasoning models can effectively detect model misbehavior such as reward hacking , and can even enable a weaker model to monitor a stronger model ( Baker et al. 2025 ). rubric.title: Monitoring Systemic Reward Hacks During Agent Training
rubric.description: This plot shows the effectiveness of different monitors in catching 'exit(0)' and 'raise SkipTest' hacks over time. Stacked area charts indicate whether both monitors, only action monitors, or only CoT monitors caught the hack, alongside instances where hacks remained uncaught.

rubric.reason: The plot is a high-quality visualization of a specific research result regarding AI safety monitoring, though the high density of overlapping areas requires careful inspection to fully grasp.

caption: When using the monitor to provide an RL reward signal to prevent reward hacking during training, the model still can find ways to hack while avoiding being caught by the monitor. (Image source: Baker et al. 2025)
context: However, incorporating CoT monitoring reward into RL does not work out well, as it leads to obfuscated reward hacking where the model tries to hide its true intent within the CoT ( Baker et al. 2025 ). With this direct optimization pressure provided by the CoT monitor applied during RL training, the model still can find ways to hack, although a bit less frequently, but can hide its intention in CoT to avoid being caught by the monitor.
section: Optimization Pressure on CoT: Good or Bad? #

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how reinforcement learning pressure on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts can lead models to hide cheating behaviors that standard monitors fail to detect.

rubric.description: Three line graphs compare a baseline agent to an agent with CoT pressure across training epochs, showing metrics for unit tests, caught cheating, and uncaught cheating. While the baseline agent's cheating is mostly caught by monitors, the CoT-pressured agent learns to cheat in ways the monitor cannot detect.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how a training collapse in accuracy corresponds with a sudden, massive increase in response length during reinforcement learning optimization.
rubric.title: Reward Hacking and CoT Length Optimization
rubric.description: Two plots show the relationship between training accuracy and response length over 120 iterations. Using a classic reward signal leads to a sharp drop in accuracy to near zero as the model learns to generate extremely long responses to maximize rewards, a phenomenon called reward hacking.

rubric.reason: The plots clearly demonstrate a cause-and-effect relationship between reward hacking (length increase) and model failure (accuracy drop) with high clarity and professional styling.

To manage computational costs, backpropagation is truncated to only the last $k$ iterations of the recurrent unit ($k=8$ in experiments), making it possible to train on the heavy-tail part of the Poisson distribution. rubric.title: Accuracy vs Test-Time Compute Recurrence
rubric.description: The plot compares model accuracy on ARC, GSM8K, and OpenBookQA benchmarks as the number of recurrent iterations (test-time compute) increases. It shows that accuracy improves significantly with more recurrence before reaching a plateau, effectively scaling the model's 'materialized parameters'.

rubric.reason: The plot is extremely clean, professional, and provides a clear insight into the trade-off between inference computation and model performance with specific saturation points.

context: Similarly, pause tokens proposed by Goyal et al. It is important to inject such pause tokens both during training and inference time, while only fine-tuning on pause tokens leads to limited gain. rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how injecting special pause tokens into an input sequence allows a transformer model to perform additional computational layers before generating a target output.
rubric.title: Pause Tokens for Computational Delay
rubric.description: Standard inference is compared to pause-inference where dummy tokens are inserted into the input sequence. These tokens trigger additional hidden layer computations while their immediate outputs are ignored, effectively giving the model more time to 'think' before producing the next real token.

caption: Illustration of Quiet-STaR. (Image source: Zelikman et al. 2025)
context: Quiet-STaR ( Zelikman et al. 2025 ) introduces token-level reasoning by training the model to generate rationales after every token to explain future text. It mixes the future-text predictions with and without rationales and uses learning to generate better rationales and uses REINFORCE to optimize the quality of rationale generation.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how a language model uses intermediate 'thought' tokens to improve next-token prediction, rewarding thoughts that help accuracy and discarding those that harm it.
rubric.title: Quiet-STaR Token-Level Reasoning Process
rubric.description: The model generates a sequence of hidden thought tokens between original text tokens to predict the next character. Correct predictions from these sampled thoughts lead to rewards and learning, while incorrect ones are discarded.

rubric.reason: The diagram clearly maps out a complex multi-step process (Think, Talk, Learn) with specific labels and logical flow, making it highly informative and easy to follow.

context: Snell et al. (2024) evaluated and compared test-time and pretraining compute, and found that they are not 1:1 exchangeable. Test-time compute can cover up the gap easily on easy and medium questions when there is only a small gap in model capability, but proves less effective for hard problems. The ratio between token budgets for pretraining and inference matters a lot. Test-time compute is only preferable when inference tokens are substantially fewer than pretraining ones. This indicates that d

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how test-time compute budgets, through iterative revisions and verifier-guided search, influence model accuracy across different question difficulties and in comparison to pretraining compute.
rubric.title: Scaling Laws for Test-Time Compute and Revision
rubric.description: Four plots show that while increasing test-time compute improves MATH accuracy, it is most effective on easy and medium questions where the ratio of inference tokens to pretraining tokens is low. The data compares iterative revision methods and PRM-based search against baseline majority voting and parallel decoding.
rubric.benchmark_query: accuracy versus generation budget for compute optimal revisions and PRM search with ratio of inference to pretraining tokens
rubric.reason: The image is dense with four distinct plots and multiple legends, requiring significant effort to parse, but it provides deep insight into the efficiency of test-time compute scaling.

caption: Both parallel and sequential scaling methods of test-time compute shows positive correlation with the evaluation performance in s1 experiments. (Image Muennighoff & Yang, et al. 2025)
context: s1 models ( Muennighoff & Yang, et al. 2025 ) experimented with scaling up the CoT reasoning path length via budget forcing technique (i.e. forcefully lengthen it by appending the word "wait" , or shorten it by terminating the model’s thinking process by appending end-of-thinking token or "Final Answer:" ). They observed a clear positive correlation between the average thinking time measured in tokens and the downstream evaluation accuracy.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how forcing longer reasoning sequences (budget forcing) and increasing total computation via majority voting improves model performance on math and science benchmarks.
rubric.title: Scaling Test-Time Compute via Sequential and Parallel Methods
rubric.description: Two plots demonstrate that accuracy on AIME24 and GPQA benchmarks increases as models are forced to generate more 'thinking' tokens or when multiple reasoning paths are sampled for majority voting. The sequential scaling plot highlights a technique where the model is forced to continue reasoning by appending the word 'Wait' when it attempts to stop.
rubric.benchmark_query: plot showing accuracy vs average thinking time tokens on AIME24 using forcing 2048/4096 max thinking tokens and appending Wait
rubric.reason: The plots clearly illustrate two distinct methods for scaling inference-time computation and their direct impact on model accuracy with helpful annotations.

caption: (Left) Longer CoT path length is positively correlated with eval accuracy. (Right) Rejection sampling for controlling the generated CoT path length shows a negative scaling where longer CoTs lead to worse eval accuracy. (Image source: Muennighoff & Yang et al. 2025)
context: When comparing this budget forcing technique with other decoding methods of controlling reasoning trace length, it is quite surprising that simple rejection sampling (i.e. sampling generation until the lengths fits a token budget) leads to reversed scaling, meaning that longer CoTs lead to worse performance.

rubric.what_it_teaches: A learner sees how increased average thinking time in tokens generally improves model accuracy on hard benchmarks, but can lead to performance degradation when forced through rejection sampling.
rubric.title: Scaling Laws for Chain of Thought Length
rubric.description: Scatter plots show a positive correlation between accuracy and thinking time tokens on MATH500, AIME24, and GPQA Diamond, while a line graph illustrates a negative trend when using rejection sampling.
rubric.benchmark_query: accuracy vs average thinking time tokens for MATH500 AIME24 GPQA Diamond and rejection sampling negative scaling
rubric.reason: The plots clearly demonstrate two opposing effects of reasoning length on model performance across specific benchmarks, making a complex empirical observation easy to grasp visually.
